standard.title: Design occupations and sustainability
standard.description: examine design and technologies occupations and factors including sustainability that impact on the design of products, services and environments to meet community needs
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify how familiar products, services and environments are designed and produced by people to meet personal or local community needs and sustainability (AC9TDE2K01). They have not yet examined occupations in design and technologies or analysed how sustainability factors actively shape design decisions.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students examine design and technologies occupations and the role sustainability plays in shaping what those occupations produce, explaining how products, services and environments are designed to meet community needs.

nodes.label: Design and technologies occupations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can name and describe a range of design and technologies occupations and explain what community need each addresses
nodes.minimum_width: Name at least two design and technologies occupations and describe what community need each one addresses
nodes.typical_width: Describe a range of design and technologies occupations across different sectors (bakers, builders, engineers, farmers, textile designers, mechanics, radiographers); explain what each occupation produces and who benefits in the community
wider: Explore how many First Nations Australians have been and continue to be recognised for specialist skills in designing and producing products from local materials — investigate specific examples and discuss how these occupations serve community needs
Survey the design and technologies occupations present in the local area (urban, suburban, regional or rural) — discuss how the mix of occupations reflects local community needs and geography
success_criteria: Names at least two distinct design and technologies occupations
Connects each occupation to a community need it addresses
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot connect occupations to community needs cannot examine in N2 and N3 how factors (including sustainability) shape what occupations produce — the factor analysis requires knowing what the occupation is trying to achieve.

nodes.label: Sustainability as a design factor
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain what sustainability means in a design context and give an example of a design decision that reflects sustainability considerations
nodes.minimum_width: Describe one example of a design decision that was shaped by sustainability (e.g. using recycled materials, minimal water use) and explain why the designer made that choice
nodes.typical_width: Explain how Australian designers consider sustainability when designing products, services and environments; describe examples across different design types (products from recycled materials, services using minimal energy, landscapes requiring minimal water)
wider: Examine how First Nations Australians use sustainable practices when designing and producing products from local materials — explore how sustainability is embedded in traditional design knowledge and how this knowledge continues today
Investigate a specific sustainability challenge in the local community (e.g. water saving, traffic management, accessibility) and examine what design factors would need to be considered to address it

response_modes.reason: Students often reduce sustainability to recycling. Examining sustainability across different design domains — products, services, environments, energy, water, materials — builds a broader and more accurate understanding of what sustainability means as a design consideration.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations sustainable design practices offer genuinely rich content — specific historical and contemporary examples (traditional adhesives, sustainable harvesting, local material use) that extend the concept well beyond the minimum while staying within band. The local community survey direction also provides meaningful contextual application.
success_criteria: Names at least one sustainability factor (e.g. recycled materials, minimal waste, energy use)
Connects that factor to a specific design decision
nodes.hinge_reason: Students without a working understanding of sustainability as a design factor cannot complete the multi-factor analysis in N3 — sustainability is one of the named factors and must be identified alongside others.

nodes.label: Factors that influence design outcomes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine a product, service or environment and identify factors (beyond sustainability) that influenced its design
nodes.minimum_width: Examine one product or environment and identify at least one factor other than sustainability that influenced how it was designed (e.g. who it is for, available materials, cost, culture)
nodes.typical_width: Examine a range of products and environments to discover the factors that shaped their design — including community need, material availability, cultural context, energy efficiency and aesthetic considerations; explain how these factors interact
wider: Examine products from an Asian country alongside Australian products — compare the design factors each reflects (materials, cultural context, production methods) and discuss why similar needs are met with different designs

Examine a system or service proposed for improvement (e.g. a water-saving bathroom system, a school traffic management system) — analyse what factors constrain the design and what factors offer opportunity for change

response_modes.reason: Students at this level can identify features of a product but need scaffolding to move from observation ('it has wheels') to design factor analysis ('wheels were chosen because the product needs to move over different surfaces'). Structured examination routines help students develop analytical habits.

This node integrates occupational knowledge (node 1) with sustainability knowledge (node 2) into a complete factor analysis — students are now examining how multiple factors interact to shape a design outcome. The coordination across factors is the learning.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one design factor beyond sustainability
Explains how that factor influenced a specific design decision
